title: useEffect
summary: **useEffect** is the React Hook for synchronizing a component with systems outside React — fetching data, subscriptions, timers, and DOM side effects — running after render and cleaning up when needed.

subtopics.title: Side effects
subtopics.explanation: A side effect is any work that reaches outside React's pure 'props/state in, JSX out' model — fetching data, subscriptions, timers, logging, or directly touching the DOM and browser APIs. Rendering itself must stay pure, so useEffect is the sanctioned escape hatch for this synchronization. The mental model is not lifecycle callbacks but 'keep this external thing in sync with these values'.

subtopics.title: Dependency array
subtopics.explanation: The dependency array tells React when to re-run the effect. With no array it runs after every render; with [] it runs once on mount; with [a, b] it runs on mount and again whenever a or b change by Object.is comparison. It should include every reactive value the effect reads — omitting one causes stale-closure bugs where the effect uses outdated values.
subtopics.example:
// runs only when userId changes
useEffect(() => { fetchUser(userId); }, [userId]);

subtopics.title: Cleanup function
subtopics.explanation: An effect can return a cleanup function that React runs before the next effect run and on unmount. This is where you tear down subscriptions, clear timers, remove event listeners, and cancel or ignore stale requests. Skipping cleanup leaks listeners and intervals and can trigger state updates on unmounted components.

subtopics.title: Mount, update, and unmount timing
subtopics.explanation: Effects run after React commits the render and the browser paints, so they don't block the visual update. On mount the setup runs; on each dependency change the previous cleanup runs first, then the new setup; on unmount the final cleanup runs. If you need to mutate the DOM before paint to avoid flicker, that's useLayoutEffect, which runs synchronously before the browser paints.

subtopics.title: Data fetching
subtopics.explanation: A typical pattern fetches in an effect, listing the relevant id as a dependency so it refetches when that changes, and tracks loading and error in state. The classic gotcha is the race condition: switching ids fast can let an earlier request resolve last and overwrite newer data. Guard against it with an ignore flag set in cleanup, or an AbortController to actually cancel the request.

subtopics.title: Stale closures
subtopics.explanation: Each render creates a new closure, so an effect captures the props and state from the render it was defined in. If you omit a value it reads from the dependency array (especially with [] 'run once'), the effect keeps using that first render's stale value forever. The react-hooks/exhaustive-deps lint rule catches these; fix the dependencies rather than suppressing the warning.
subtopics.example:
// stale: captures userId from first render only
useEffect(() => { load(userId); }, []); // should be [userId]

subtopics.title: Infinite loops
subtopics.explanation: Omitting the dependency array on an effect that updates state creates an infinite loop: the effect sets state, which triggers a render, which runs the effect again, and so on. Similarly, an unstable dependency — a new object, array, or function created every render — makes the effect re-run constantly. Stabilize references with useMemo or useCallback, or provide a correct dependency array.
subtopics.example:
// infinite loop: no array + setState every render
useEffect(() => { setData(Date.now()); });

subtopics.title: When NOT to use useEffect
subtopics.explanation: A top code-review issue is using effects for things derivable during render — like computing a filtered list or formatting a value — which adds an extra render and a sync bug surface. Compute derived data during render instead, and reserve effects for genuine synchronization with external systems. For serious data fetching, a library like React Query or SWR handles caching, deduplication, and cancellation far better than hand-rolled effects.

foundations.overview: useEffect lets a function component run side effects — work that reaches outside the pure 'props/state in, JSX out' model. After React renders and commits to the DOM, it runs your effect. You declare which values the effect depends on; React re-runs it when any of them change, and runs an optional cleanup before the next run and on unmount.
foundations.formalDefinition: useEffect(setup, dependencies) registers a side effect. `setup` runs after the render is committed; it may return a `cleanup` function. With a dependency array, the effect runs after the first render and again whenever a listed dependency changes by Object.is comparison; with `[]` it runs once on mount; with no array it runs after every render.
foundations.whyItMatters: Rendering must be pure, but real apps must talk to the outside world: servers, timers, browser APIs, subscriptions. useEffect is the sanctioned escape hatch for that synchronization, and getting its dependencies and cleanup right is one of the most-tested skills in React.
foundations.mentalModel: Don't think of useEffect as lifecycle callbacks. Think of it as: 'keep this external thing in sync with these values.' You describe what to synchronize and what it depends on; React decides when to run and clean up so the outside world matches your current state and props.
foundations.browserPerspective: Effects run after the browser has painted the committed DOM, so they don't block the visual update. A subscription, fetch, or timer started in an effect lives outside React; the cleanup function is what tears it down so you don't leak listeners or intervals as the component re-renders or unmounts.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Fetching data when an id prop changes, subscribing to a WebSocket or event emitter, setting up intervals/timeouts, syncing to localStorage, reading element size, and updating document.title.
foundations.businessImpact: Effects power the dynamic data that users actually came for. Bugs here — duplicate fetches, leaked subscriptions, runaway loops — degrade performance, inflate API costs, and cause flickering or stale UI that frustrates users.
foundations.engineeringImpact: A correct dependency array and cleanup function prevent an entire family of bugs: stale data, memory leaks, infinite loops, and race conditions between overlapping fetches. Misusing useEffect (for derived state, for example) is a top code-review issue.
foundations.performanceImpact: Each effect re-runs whenever its dependencies change, so an unstable dependency (a new object/array/function every render) can cause excessive work or infinite loops. Cleaning up subscriptions and aborting in-flight fetches keeps the app from doing redundant or wasteful work.
commonUseCases: Fetching data when a prop like an id changes
Subscribing/unsubscribing to events, sockets, or stores
Syncing state to localStorage or updating document.title

commonMisconceptions.myth: useEffect runs during rendering, before paint.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It runs after the render is committed and the browser paints. If you need to mutate the DOM before paint, that's useLayoutEffect, not useEffect.

commonMisconceptions.myth: An empty dependency array means 'never re-run, so I can omit anything'.
commonMisconceptions.reality: [] means 'run once on mount'. If the effect uses props/state, they belong in the dependency array; omitting them causes stale-closure bugs where the effect uses outdated values.

visualExplorer.title: Render → commit → effect → cleanup
visualExplorer.caption: Follow one render cycle: React renders, commits to the DOM, the browser paints, then the effect runs. On the next dependency change, cleanup runs before the new effect.

interactiveExamples.title: Sync the document title to state
interactiveExamples.explanation: The effect runs after render and whenever count changes (it's in the dependency array), keeping the tab title in sync with state.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: The page shows the count, and the browser tab title updates to match every time you click +1.

interactiveExamples.title: A timer with cleanup
interactiveExamples.explanation: The effect starts an interval on mount and returns a cleanup that clears it on unmount. Without the cleanup, the interval would keep firing and leak.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A counter that increments once per second, driven by an interval that is cleaned up when the component unmounts.

codeLab.title: Fetch on mount with loading state
codeLab.instructions: Use useEffect with an empty dependency array to fetch a random number once on mount. Track loading and value in state, show 'Loading…' while the promise is pending, then display the value. Use a fake async function provided in the starter.
codeLab.expectedOutput: Shows 'Loading…' briefly, then displays a random number fetched once on mount.
hints: Initialise loading to true and value to null with useState.
Call fakeFetch().then(...) inside the effect and set both state values; use an `active` flag in cleanup to ignore a late resolve after unmount.

debuggingLab.title: The missing dependency that causes a stale value (and a loop)
debuggingLab.symptom: Two bugs at once: the effect that should refetch when `userId` changes never updates after the first render, and a second effect that omits its array refetches on every single render, hammering the API.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: The first effect reads `userId` but lists `[]`, so it captures userId=1 from the first render and never re-runs — the classic missing-dependency stale-closure bug. The second effect has no dependency array, so it runs after every render; because it calls setData (a state update), every run schedules another render, which runs the effect again — an infinite loop. React's lint rule (react-hooks/exhaustive-deps) flags exactly these.
commonMistakes: Leaving values the effect uses out of the dependency array (especially with [] 'run once').
Omitting the dependency array entirely on an effect that sets state, creating an infinite render loop.
Disabling the exhaustive-deps lint warning instead of fixing the real dependency.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Make the data-loading effect depend on `userId` so it re-runs when the id changes, and remove the second always-running effect (or give it a correct dependency array) so it no longer loops.

theory.question: What does the dependency array control, and what's the difference between omitting it, passing [], and passing [a, b]?
theory.directAnswer: The dependency array tells React when to re-run the effect. With no array, the effect runs after every render. With [], it runs only once after mount (and cleans up on unmount). With [a, b], it runs after mount and again whenever a or b change (compared with Object.is). The dependency list should include every reactive value the effect reads.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A list of reactive values (props, state, derived values) that, when changed, should cause the effect to re-run and re-synchronize.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Effects synchronize external systems with your data. The array lets React skip re-running an effect when nothing it depends on has changed, avoiding wasted work and incorrect updates.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: After each render React compares each dependency to its previous value with Object.is. If any differs, it runs the cleanup from the prior effect, then runs the effect again.

theory.whyImportant: Dependency-array reasoning is the heart of useEffect and the source of most React bugs (stale closures, loops). Interviewers use it to test whether you truly understand React's model.
theory.realWorldExample: An effect that fetches a profile lists [userId]; switching users re-runs the fetch, but typing in an unrelated field does not.

nestedTopics.title: Run once vs every render
nestedTopics.explanation: [] runs once on mount; no array runs after every render — rarely what you want.

nestedTopics.title: Exhaustive deps
nestedTopics.explanation: The react-hooks/exhaustive-deps lint rule warns when an effect reads a value not in its array, catching stale-closure bugs early.

nestedTopics.title: Object.is comparison
nestedTopics.explanation: Dependencies are compared by identity, so a new object/array/function each render counts as 'changed' even if its contents are equal.

followUps.question: Why might a function dependency cause an effect to re-run every render?
followUps.answer: A function defined inside the component is a new reference each render. Wrap it in useCallback (or move it out / into the effect) to stabilize the reference.

followUps.question: Is it ever OK to omit a dependency?
followUps.answer: Only when the value is provably stable (e.g. a setter from useState, which React guarantees is stable). Otherwise include it or restructure the effect.

scenario.question: Users report that when they switch quickly between two profiles, the page sometimes shows the wrong profile's data. What is happening and how do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: It's a race condition between overlapping fetches: switching profiles starts a new fetch before the previous one resolves, and whichever resolves last wins — sometimes the stale one. The fix is to cancel or ignore the stale request in the effect's cleanup, using an `ignore` flag or an AbortController so only the latest fetch is applied.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A data-fetching race where multiple in-flight requests for different dependencies resolve out of order.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Each dependency change starts a new effect run with its own async request; React doesn't know the earlier request is now irrelevant unless you tell it.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: On each run you set a local `ignore = false`; the cleanup sets `ignore = true`. When a fetch resolves you only apply its result if ignore is still false, so superseded responses are dropped. An AbortController can additionally cancel the network request.

scenario.whyImportant: Race conditions in effects are extremely common in real apps and a favorite interview scenario because the naive fetch-in-effect code looks correct but is subtly broken.

nestedTopics.title: Cleanup as cancellation
nestedTopics.explanation: The cleanup function runs before the next effect, making it the right place to invalidate the previous request.

nestedTopics.title: AbortController
nestedTopics.explanation: Passing controller.signal to fetch lets you actually abort the network call, not just ignore the result.

followUps.question: Would a data-fetching library help here?
followUps.answer: Yes — libraries like React Query or SWR handle cancellation, caching, and race conditions for you, which is why teams often prefer them over hand-written effects.

coding.question: Build a component that tracks the window width and updates live as the user resizes, cleaning up the listener on unmount.
coding.thoughtProcess: I need to subscribe to the window 'resize' event. I store width in state, add the listener in an effect with [] so it's set up once, update state in the handler, and return a cleanup that removes the listener so it doesn't leak after unmount.
coding.lineByLine: useState(window.innerWidth) seeds the initial width. The effect runs once ([]), adds a resize listener that updates state, and returns a cleanup that removes the listener. The cleanup runs on unmount, preventing a leaked listener that would keep calling setWidth on an unmounted component.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) per resize event for the state update.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) — a single listener and one number in state.

alternativeApproaches.title: Extract a useWindowWidth hook
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Move this logic into a custom hook so multiple components can reuse the subscription-with-cleanup pattern, keeping components clean.

followUps.question: Why include the cleanup if the page reloads anyway?
followUps.answer: Components mount and unmount constantly within a single-page app; without cleanup, stale listeners accumulate and call setState on unmounted components, leaking memory and causing warnings.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Use effects only for true synchronization with external systems (network, subscriptions, browser APIs). Extract reusable patterns into custom hooks (useFetch, useWindowWidth). For data fetching at scale, prefer a dedicated library (React Query, SWR) over hand-rolled effects.
productionDeepDive.performance: Keep dependency arrays accurate and dependencies stable (useCallback/useMemo where needed) so effects re-run only when necessary. Always clean up timers, listeners, and subscriptions to avoid leaks and redundant work.
productionDeepDive.security: When fetching in effects, validate and escape responses before rendering. Use AbortController to cancel requests on unmount so responses for a screen the user already left aren't processed. Never put secrets in client-side effect code.
productionDeepDive.scaling: As features grow, ad-hoc fetch-in-effect code multiplies race conditions and cache-invalidation bugs. Centralizing data fetching in a query library or a service layer keeps behavior consistent and reduces duplicated effect logic.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Don't use effects for things derivable during render — that's a code smell. Keep each effect focused on one concern, and trust the exhaustive-deps lint rule instead of suppressing it.
productionDeepDive.observability: React DevTools and the React Profiler show when effects run and re-render; in StrictMode (dev) React intentionally mounts, unmounts, and remounts components to surface missing cleanups, so leaks show up early.

caseStudies.problem: Hand-written fetch-in-useEffect code across the app caused duplicate requests, race conditions, and stale data.
caseStudies.solution: Adopted React Query to handle caching, deduplication, and cancellation, removing most bespoke effects.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: A new dependency and learning curve vs dramatically fewer data-fetching bugs and less boilerplate.
caseStudies.lessons: Effects are a low-level primitive; for data fetching, a purpose-built library usually beats reinventing cancellation and caching by hand.

projectBuilder.summary: Wire the dashboard to live data and browser APIs using effects: fetch users on mount, refetch when a selected filter changes, and persist the active tab to localStorage.
requirements: Fetch the user list once on mount with loading and error states
Refetch when the selected status filter changes (dependency array)
Persist the active tab to localStorage and restore it on reload
projectBuilder.architecture: Hold users, loading, and error in state. One effect fetches when the filter dependency changes, using an ignore flag in cleanup to avoid race conditions. A second small effect syncs the active tab to localStorage whenever it changes.

src/
  hooks/
    useUsers.js
  components/
    UsersTable.jsx
    StatusFilter.jsx
  pages/
    Dashboard.jsx

steps.title: Fetch on mount
steps.instructions: Add an effect with [] that loads users and toggles loading; show a spinner until it resolves.
steps.checkpoint: Users load once when the page mounts.

steps.title: Refetch on filter change
steps.instructions: Add the status filter to the effect's dependency array and use an ignore flag in cleanup so only the latest fetch is applied.
steps.checkpoint: Changing the filter refetches without showing stale data.

steps.title: Persist the active tab
steps.instructions: Add a separate effect that writes the active tab to localStorage on change, and initialise state from localStorage on first render.
steps.checkpoint: Reloading the page restores the last active tab.

enhancements: Replace the hand-written fetch with React Query
Add an AbortController to cancel in-flight requests on filter change
interviewQuestions: Why does the fetch effect need a cleanup function when the filter changes rapidly?
Why is persisting to localStorage done in an effect rather than during render?

keyTakeaways: useEffect runs side effects after render and commit, not during rendering.
The dependency array controls re-runs: [] = once on mount, [a] = when a changes, none = every render.
Return a cleanup function to tear down subscriptions, timers, and listeners and to cancel stale fetches.
Missing dependencies cause stale-closure bugs; a missing array plus a state update causes infinite loops.
Trust the exhaustive-deps lint rule, and reach for a data library for serious fetching.
